articles.title: Healey vows cheaper marmalade and gherkins in pre-Budget package of 'everyday fixes'
articles.description: The chancellor will axe tariffs on some staples as part of plans to give households "breathing space".
articles.summary: John Healey will remove import taxes on marmalade, gherkins and more than 100 products in a bid to give families "breathing space" with the cost of living at the Budget .
key_points: The chancellor on Wednesday will promise a fresh series of "everyday fixes" to ease the pressure on households.
The measures will also include an end to the so-called cliff-edge for those receiving carer's allowance payments and higher tax-free mileage rates being made permanent.
But the Conservatives said the offer of "cheaper gherkins" was "an insult to families hammered by Labour's tax rises".

articles.description: Changes are needed to prevent the full, flat-rate state pension becoming liable for income tax after it rises in April.
articles.summary: Pensioners on low incomes will be shielded from income tax by Chancellor John Healey in his first Budget on Wednesday.
key_points: The full, flat-rate state pension is expected to increase by 3.9% to £13,036.40 a year from April.
This would take the payment above the £12,570 personal tax allowance and therefore be liable for income tax if no changes are made.
The government had already committed to not taxing people who only get an income from the state pension.

articles.title: Healey's Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds
articles.description: The economic is positive now but come January things could become trickier for the Labour government
articles.summary: The chancellor's aides are using intelligence-style security measures to guard its secrets: the Budget has been split into "compartments" with very few given access to all of them.
key_points: The IT has been locked down and ministers viewing the plans have to sign a digital promise not to brief media.
Such security is a response to the feeling that speculation around the last Budget, sometimes informed by insiders, was economically destabilising.

As a recent former defence secretary, Chancellor John Healey has embraced such strict procedures, and has approached most of his public engagements and interviews with a sturdy refusal to break the Budget omertà,…

articles.title: Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing
articles.description: Data centres are the lifeblood of our digital world, but there are growing concerns about their environmental impact. The BBC explores their rise in charts.
articles.summary: Until a few years ago many of us may have been blissfully unaware of what a data centre was.
key_points: These giant, warehouse-like buildings power virtually all our internet activity, from our web searches and emails to movie downloads and online banking.
They are at the heart of the AI boom, housing the advanced computer chips and servers needed to run services like ChatGPT and Claude.
But the speed at which they're growing, the enormous amount of electricity they consume and concerns about their environmental impact are fuelling a public backlash around the world.
